summary: Segment Routing encodes an end-to-end path as a list of segments, and can run over MPLS or IPv6. This document describes the OSPFv3 extensions needed to support Segment Routing over the IPv6 data plane.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment Routing is a list of stops for a trip. This lets the network's road-map system, OSPFv3, share those stops when the trip uses IPv6.

questions: how does ospfv3 advertise srv6 sids
what is an srv6 end.x sid
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers tell each other about their SRv6 locators, segment IDs and limits.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) steers packets with lists of 128-bit segment IDs, but OSPFv3 had no way to advertise which SRv6 features, locators and segment IDs each router has.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9513 adds an SRv6 Capabilities TLV, a new SRv6 Locator LSA (function code 42) that carries locators and End SIDs, and End.X SID sub-TLVs for links and neighbors.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 can now distribute everything SRv6 needs inside a network. It is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9513 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2023, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the OSPFv3 counterpart of the IS-IS extensions in RFC 9352, and it points to RFC 9514 for learning these SIDs through BGP-LS.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
The Segment Routing (SR) architecture, described in RFC 8402, lets a node steer a packet with an ordered list of instructions called segments. Each segment is named by a Segment Identifier (SID). When SR runs on the IPv6 data plane through the Segment Routing Header defined in RFC 8754, it is called SRv6. RFC 8986 describes how behaviors are bound to SIDs, and this document assumes the reader knows it.

RFC 9513 specifies the OSPFv3 extensions that carry SRv6 information. The extensions have four parts: an SRv6 Capabilities TLV, sub-TLVs for several Maximum SID Depths, an SRv6 Locator TLV carried in a new SRv6 Locator Link State Advertisement (LSA), and TLVs and sub-TLVs that advertise SIDs together with their Endpoint behaviors.
sections.plainLanguage: SRv6 is a trip plan made of stops. OSPFv3 is the system routers use to share maps, and this RFC teaches it to share the list of stops too.

sections.title: Capabilities and Maximum SID Depths
sections.content:
An SRv6-enabled router MUST advertise the SRv6 Capabilities TLV (type 20) as an optional top-level TLV of the OSPFv3 Router Information LSA. It appears only once, and area-scoped flooding is REQUIRED for it. Its Flags field has one defined bit, the O-flag, which says the router supports the O-flag in the SRH flags described in RFC 9259. No sub-TLVs are defined for it. If a receiver sees several copies, it uses the first one, preferring the area-scoped Router Information LSA.

Supported algorithms are advertised with the SR-Algorithm TLV from RFC 8665, as described in RFC 8666. Limits on how the router handles the SRH are advertised as Maximum SID Depth (MSD) types, reusing the SRv6 MSD types defined for IS-IS in RFC 9352 and the mechanism of RFC 8476.

  • Maximum Segments Left: the largest Segments Left value the router accepts before applying a SID's behavior; if not advertised, 0 is assumed.
  • Maximum End Pop: the most SIDs in the SRH to which the router can apply the Penultimate Segment Pop or Ultimate Segment Pop flavors.
  • Maximum H.Encaps: the most SIDs that can be added by the H.Encaps behavior.
  • Maximum End D: the most SIDs in an SRH when the router decapsulates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router tells its neighbors what tricks it knows and how long a list of stops it can handle, so nobody hands it a list that is too long.

sections.title: SIDs, Locators and Reachability
sections.content:
An SRv6 SID is 128 bits and has locator, function and argument parts. A router is given one locator per algorithm it supports, and each locator is a covering prefix for all SIDs on that router that use the same algorithm. Locators MUST be advertised in an SRv6 Locator TLV inside an SRv6 Locator LSA, which is used instead of the Extended Prefix LSAs of RFC 8362 to keep ordinary prefix reachability separate from SRv6 locator reachability.

Receiving routers install forwarding entries for locators whose algorithm they support. SIDs themselves are not directly routable and MUST NOT be installed in the forwarding plane; they are reached through a covering locator. Locators for algorithms 0 and 1 SHOULD also be advertised as ordinary prefixes so that routers without SRv6 support still forward the traffic. If a locator arrives both ways, the ordinary prefix advertisement MUST be preferred when installing forwarding entries. Locators tied to Flexible Algorithms SHOULD NOT be advertised in the base prefix advertisements, following RFC 9350.

Prefixes and locators can be marked anycast with the AC-bit (value 0x80) in PrefixOptions. All nodes advertising the same anycast locator MUST instantiate exactly the same set of SIDs under it, otherwise traffic may be dropped or misrouted.

Correct forwarding relies on the SID's own locator being the longest prefix match. A default or summary route, or a different locator or prefix that matches longer, can break this.
sections.plainLanguage: A locator is like a street name, and a SID is a house number on that street. Routers learn how to reach the street, and the house number only makes sense once you are on it.

sections.title: The SRv6 Locator LSA and TLV
sections.content:
The SRv6 Locator LSA has OSPFv3 LSA function code 42. Its flooding scope is chosen by the advertising router through the S1/S2 bits, and the U-bit is set so the LSA is flooded even by routers that do not understand it. A router can send several such LSAs, told apart by their Link State IDs. The body holds TLVs in the format of RFC 3630, padded to 4-octet alignment.

The top-level SRv6 Locator TLV (type 1) carries a Route Type, an Algorithm, a Locator Length (1 to 128 bits), PrefixOptions, a 4-octet Metric and the locator itself as an IPv6 prefix of 1 to 16 octets. A metric of 0xFFFFFFFF means unreachable. A TLV with a route type other than the six listed MUST be ignored. Sub-TLVs from the Extended Prefix family, such as Route-Tag and the Prefix Source sub-TLVs of RFC 9084, may be used inside it.
sections.plainLanguage: The Locator LSA is a notice board. Each notice names a street, says how far away it is, and lists the special stops on it.

sections.title: Advertising End SIDs and End.X SIDs
sections.content:
An SRv6 End SID sub-TLV (type 1) sits inside the SRv6 Locator TLV. It carries an Endpoint Behavior code point from RFC 8986 and the 16-octet SID. Every SRv6-enabled router SHOULD advertise at least one End SID for itself. The SID inherits the algorithm of its parent locator and MUST be allocated from that locator; otherwise it is ignored.

SIDs tied to a link or neighbor are different. The SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV (type 31) and the SRv6 LAN End.X SID sub-TLV (type 32) are carried in the E-Router-Link TLV. The first covers point-to-point and point-to-multipoint links and the adjacency to the Designated Router on broadcast and NBMA links. The LAN version adds the 4-octet Neighbor Router-ID for the Backup DR and DR-Other neighbors. Both have Algorithm and Weight fields and flags B (backup), S (set of adjacencies) and P (persistent). Every router SHOULD instantiate at least one End.X SID per neighbor unless features such as TE or TI-LFA are not in use, and each such SID MUST fall within a locator with the matching algorithm advertised by the same router.

An optional SID Structure sub-TLV (type 30, length always 4) gives the bit lengths of the locator block, locator node, function and argument parts, which must add up to at most 128 bits. It is for control and management use only and MUST NOT be used by a transit node for forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: An End SID is a stop at a router itself, and an End.X SID is a stop that says go out through this particular door to that neighbor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions do not change the existing OSPFv3 security considerations of RFC 5340. Authentication is RECOMMENDED for OSPFv3 deployments, and RFC 7166 describes an alternative to IPsec for it. Malformed TLVs or sub-TLVs SHOULD be counted or logged in a rate-limited manner.

The security considerations of SR in RFC 8402 and of SRv6 network programming in RFC 8986 also apply. The RFC also warns that advertising an incorrect MSD value may have negative consequences, and points to RFC 9259 for the O-flag and RFC 9350 for Flexible Algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Since routers trust what their neighbors announce, you should make sure only real neighbors can post notices, and keep a note of notices that look broken.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA assigned several code points: type 20 for the SRv6 Capabilities TLV in the OSPF Router Information TLVs registry, function code 42 for the SRv6 Locator LSA, and the AC-bit (0x80) in the OSPFv3 Prefix Options registry. In the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry it assigned 30 (SID Structure), 31 (End.X SID) and 32 (LAN End.X SID).

It also created new registries: flags for the SRv6 Capabilities TLV, the End SID sub-TLV and the Adjacency SID sub-TLVs, plus registries of SRv6 Locator LSA TLVs and Sub-TLVs. Notes added to the two sub-TLV registries require new allocations in one to be checked for use in the other.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the official list of numbers. This RFC asked for a few new numbers and new empty lists for future ones.
